in_text_mentions: The combination of peripheral consolidation at imaging, blood eosinophilia, and BAL eosinophilia (Figure 3), and response to steroid treatment are often sufficient for the diagnosis, avoiding the need to perform lung biopsy. However, it is sometimes difficult to differentiate CEP from organizing pneumonia (OP) because eosinophils could be slightly increased in BAL of cryptogenic OP and HRCT features may be similar. However, in CEP, consolidations are less frequently peribronchovascular and less frequently show a reverse halo sign, as compared to OP (19–22).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Panel A is a real chest radiograph from a patient whose article title identifies chronic eosinophilic pneumonia; the caption describes bilateral interstitial opacities, and although classic CEP shows peripheral infiltrates, the article title calls the presentation atypical with overlapping emphysema and fibrosis. B: Panel B is an axial chest CT panel showing ground-glass opacities, right apical hyperdensities with air bronchograms, and subpleural lesions, which can be CEP-related CT manifestations; the article title describes an atypical CEP presentation with emphysema and fibrosis. C: Panel C is another axial chest CT panel showing ground-glass opacities with central and peripheral distribution, right apical hyperdensities with air bronchograms, and subpleural lesions; these are compatible with CEP, though the article describes atypical overlap with emphysema and fibrosis.

panels.rationale: Single-panel chest X-ray (PA, February 2018) from a case series of chronic eosinophilic pneumonia and allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis. The caption describes bilateral perihilar peribronchial cuffing with diffuse bilateral alveolar shadows (right greater than left), and the image visibly shows bilateral perihilar patchy alveolar opacities, confirming an abnormal film. Prior caption triage and the clinical context (negative Aspergillus fumigatus IgE) support attribution to chronic eosinophilic pneumonia rather than ABPA. The perihilar-predominant distribution deviates from the classic peripheral (photographic-negative-of-pulmonary-edema) CEP pattern, so it is classified as a variant radiographic presentation. Note: one in-text sentence states 'Chest x-ray was normal (Fig. 6)', which conflicts with both the caption and the visibly abnormal image; the caption and image are treated as authoritative. No age or ethnicity is stated for this figure.
